title: The Assurance Bench
blurb: Six pre-release assurance disciplines that stand between a finished model and a launch decision. Sort each scene into the discipline it's exercising.
source: AIGP BOK III.C · AIGP Study Guide (SG) §Domain III.C (Periodic Assurance; Incident/Issue/Risk Management)
hint: These are pre-release, development-cycle checks. Ask what stage the scene is in: a paper catalog before any test runs is threat modeling; a live attempt to break the system is red teaming; an independent reviewer checking the evidence trail is an audit.
note: Everything on this board happens before or during the readiness decision. What a live system owes its operator after launch, on a recurring basis, is a different board.

zones.name: Audit
zones.def: An independent reviewer, organizationally separate from the team that built the system, checks the technical file — data provenance, testing records, impact assessments — against a named standard or policy and produces a report of gaps with owners and deadlines. The evidence trail, not a live attack.

zones.name: Red teaming
zones.def: Specialists simulate a realistic adversary or misuse scenario end-to-end — jailbreaks, prompt injection, social engineering, edge-case abuse — to see how the whole system holds up under pressure, then feed what they found back into a remediation plan that gets re-tested.

zones.name: Threat modeling
zones.def: A structured, paper-based exercise, done at design time before any test runs, that catalogs what needs protecting, who might attack it, and which abuse cases matter most — producing a list of risks and named mitigations, not a live attempt to exploit anything.

zones.name: Security testing
zones.def: Hands-on probing of specific, already-identified components — the serving API, dependencies, the pipeline's code — to confirm a defense is actually present and correctly configured, distinct from a full-system adversarial simulation or a paper catalog of what could go wrong.

zones.name: Post-market monitoring
zones.def: The technical cadence of checks — scheduled evaluations, tracked metrics, automated alerts — that gets built and rehearsed as the monitoring plan comes together. The dashboards and detectors themselves, not the standing legal duty to run them once the system is live.

zones.name: Incident response
zones.def: The formal, time-boxed machinery — containment first, then root-cause analysis, then corrective action — that activates the moment a scene involves confirmed real-world harm, not a routine finding still being logged and watched.

items.label: An independent reviewer, organizationally separate from the product team, checks fairness distributions and data-provenance records against ISO/IEC 42001 before sign-off.
items.why: Independence from the build team plus a documented evidence trail is this discipline's signature — distinct from red teaming, where the same independence is used to attack the system rather than review its paperwork.

items.label: The most crucial output isn't a benchmark score but a prioritized list of non-conformities, each with a named owner and a remediation deadline.
items.why: An audit's deliverable is a gap-and-fix ledger against the paper trail — different from threat modeling's abuse-case catalog, which lists what could happen rather than what already went wrong.

items.label: A week before scheduled launch, a final internal review of the technical file turns up a fairness gap that earlier uniform-sample testing had missed.
items.why: Reviewing the record after the fact to catch what testing missed is this discipline's job — the earlier testing itself, and any red-team exercise that already ran and closed, belong to their own zones.

items.label: Hired specialists chain jailbreak prompts to get past the guardrails before launch; findings feed the risk register and are re-tested once fixed.
items.why: Simulating realistic misuse end-to-end is the discipline's job — a pen test only probes infrastructure, and an audit would review the resulting report, not go find the exploit itself.

items.label: Testers push a customer-service chatbot through social-engineering framing, prompt injection and edge-case misuse scenarios that no ordinary QA script would try.
items.why: Multi-perspective adversarial simulation combining technical attacks with misuse framing is the discipline's greatest governance value — a component-level probe of one API endpoint stays in the next zone instead.

items.label: A rare-condition failure that only shows up under specific weather and lighting conditions surfaces during pre-launch adversarial testing; release is delayed until the scenario is fixed and revalidated, however rare the trigger.
items.why: Live adversarial testing is what surfaced this failure in the first place — a threat-modeling exercise would only have flagged it as a hypothetical scenario on paper, never actually run it.

items.label: Assets, trust boundaries and abuse cases are enumerated on the architecture diagram at design time, before any test runs.
items.why: Structured anticipation on paper, with no live attacking, is what makes this discipline preventive rather than diagnostic — the moment someone actually tries the jailbreak, the work has moved to red teaming.

items.label: The design review lists possible adversaries, their goals and capabilities, alongside the safeguard each abuse case will need — no live attack attempted yet.
items.why: A named-owner, mitigation-linked catalog is the deliverable here — distinct from security testing, which only starts once a specific safeguard needs to be confirmed as actually working.

items.label: The map catalogs which datasets, libraries and pre-trained weights could be tampered with along the supply chain, and names an owner for each safeguard — the exercise happens before the system ships.
items.why: Cataloging what could be tampered with is anticipation, not verification — confirming that a dependency scan actually caught a compromised library is a different, hands-on discipline.

items.label: Pen testers hit the serving API and admin console for misconfigurations and weak authentication, a dependency scan flags outdated libraries, and rate limits are checked under simulated load.
items.why: Hands-on probing of specific, already-identified components confirms a defense actually works — threat modeling only mapped where these weak points might be, it never ran the check.

items.label: A line-by-line review of the preprocessing pipeline checks for injection risks and exposed secrets, while an inventory tracks every library and dataset the release depends on.
items.why: Confirming that a specific, named component is hardened is narrower than red teaming's full-stack, end-to-end misuse simulation — this discipline stays inside one component at a time.

items.label: The API pen-test and dependency-scan findings get logged with a severity, an owner and a re-test deadline, and the release can't sign off until they close.
items.why: Probe, patch, re-test is this discipline's operating loop against a defined component — an audit would instead review whether that loop happened at all, rather than run it.

items.label: Weekly shadow evaluations replay recent traffic against a reference model, and monthly fairness checks run on the cadence the launch plan set out.
items.why: This is the technical cadence-and-dashboard side of the monitoring plan; the standing legal duty to run it at all, once the system is live, belongs to a different board entirely.

items.label: The product team's own dashboard tracks calibration and latency against a validated baseline on a running weekly cadence, with fairness disparity ratios refreshing automatically alongside them.
items.why: A continuous, automated feed owned by the team that built the system is this zone's texture — the moment that same check is instead run by a reviewer organizationally separate from that team, on a scheduled visit rather than a live feed, it's an audit.

items.label: Automated telemetry watches for anomalous traffic patterns and crafted inputs meant to confuse the model, and raises an alert when either crosses a threshold.
items.why: An automated, always-on watch is this zone's texture — a scheduled, hands-on probe of the same interfaces to confirm the defense holds is the pen-testing discipline instead.

items.label: During a pre-launch pilot with a small group of real users, real-world harm is confirmed — the moment it is, containment begins immediately: isolate first, investigate second, with the GDPR 72-hour notification clock already running.
items.why: Confirmed harm is this discipline's trigger, whether the system is still in a gated pilot or fully live; a pattern of low-severity mispredictions still being logged and watched for a trend hasn't crossed that line yet, and stays in routine issue tracking.

items.label: Mid-pilot, before general availability, a customer-service chatbot issues unsafe medical guidance to one of the trial users; the finding triggers a formal playbook — a severity tag, clear escalation roles, and a root-cause analysis that must finish before the case can close.
items.why: The formal, time-boxed machinery — severity, ownership, a defined close-out — spins up the moment harm actually lands on a real person, pilot or not, unlike an audit's scheduled review of records that may show nothing wrong at all.

items.label: Before the pilot converts to general availability, a blameless retrospective on the confirmed-harm case still assigns concrete fixes — retraining on corrected data, tighter rate limits, an updated model card — with evidence preserved for forensics.
items.why: Turning a confirmed harm into durable fixes and a preserved evidence trail closes this discipline's loop, whether the harm surfaced in a gated pilot or full production — feeding a finding into the risk register without that harm having occurred yet is threat modeling's job instead.
